entries.content:
Prof. Sashikumaar Ganesan

Founder, ZenteiQ

Fisayo Feyisetan

Product Manager, Google Kubernetes Engine

Today we hear from ZenteiQ, an artificial intelligence startup spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and selected under the IndiaAI Mission to build sovereign scientific foundation models from the ground up. To pre-train models that understand physical laws, governing equations, and numerical solvers, ZenteiQ designed and built a large-scale batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that runs across multiple model families and feeds verified datasets into training runs. Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and GKE Inference Gateway gave ZenteiQ the inference-routing layer within its pipeline to scale aggregate inference throughput 4.07x and grow daily output from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion generated tokens for every 1,000 accelerators. - Fisayo Feyisetan, Product Manager, Google Cloud

Unlike general-purpose language models trained primarily on web text and code, scientific foundation models must understand complex physical systems, mathematical governing equations, and numerical solvers across domains such as thermodynamics, computational fluid dynamics, and electromagnetics. At ZenteiQ, we are building sovereign scientific foundation models from scratch that interpret simulation outputs, evaluate equation formulations, and work through step-by-step mathematical derivations that obey physical laws.

Pre-training models on large datasets of governing equations takes hundreds of billions of reasoning tokens. Alongside curated scientific literature and simulation datasets, we also rely on a batch synthetic data-generation pipeline that we independently designed and implemented to generate, evaluate, and filter candidate derivations and solver validation problems before feeding them into our MaxText pre-training jobs.

Because we operate on a fixed compute allocation, every hour our accelerators spend generating and verifying training data is an hour taken away from pre-training. When data generation falls behind, multi-host accelerator clusters reserved for pre-training sit idle, waiting on datasets.

When data generation slows down pre-training

To maximize data generation speed, our pipeline separates prompt preparation on worker pods from model serving on vLLM across multi-node accelerator pools. Each batch moves through four stages: expanding scientific seed concepts into prompt batches, generating candidate reasoning traces with generator models, scoring responses using evaluator models, and running guardrail checks with a separate model family before packaging verified datasets for pre-training.

We originally ran these model pools on Kubernetes with standard ClusterIP round-robin load balancing across inference endpoints. As we scaled our pipeline to feed our 9B- and 35B-parameter model schedules, two routing bottlenecks began slowing down dataset creation.

  • Uneven engine queues: Our upstream worker pods expand seed concepts into prompts of widely varying complexity and response length. Because standard round-robin load balancing had no visibility into vLLM engine queues, it kept sending new requests to serving pods that were already busy processing long reasoning traces, while neighboring nodes had capacity to spare.
  • Redundant prefix computation: Prompts within a generation batch share roughly 70% to 80% of their instructional context and task specifications. Round-robin routing scattered requests with identical instructions across different serving instances, forcing each pod to recompute the same shared prompt prefix from scratch instead of reusing warm caches in accelerator memory.

Together, uneven queues and redundant prefill work caused our generation throughput to swing by as much as half within a single run, stretching out dataset creation and delaying the start of scheduled pre-training runs. We needed routing that understood live vLLM queue depths and prompt caches, without pulling our researchers off model development to build and maintain a custom inference scheduler.

Building on GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d

We already run our data preparation and MaxText pre-training jobs on GKE, which lets our team manage data generation and model training on the same Kubernetes platform. Following a recommendation from Google Cloud to address our routing bottlenecks without changing our underlying scientific methodology or pipeline design, we deployed GKE Inference Gateway, powered by the open-source llm-d distributed inference framework, in front of our vLLM accelerator pools.

In our pipeline, worker pods pull scientific seed documents and domain taxonomies from Cloud Storage and expand them into batches of multi-step prompts. Those batches flow through a single GKE Inference Gateway deployment that manages traffic across all of our model families and serving nodes.

Rather than maintaining isolated routing for each model tier, we route generation requests, evaluation queries, and guardrail checks across their respective model pools through the same gateway. Once candidate responses pass evaluation and guardrail checks, worker pods deduplicate and package the verified datasets for direct consumption by downstream MaxText pre-training jobs on GKE.

GKE Inference Gateway routes batch generation, evaluation, and guardrail requests across multi-node accelerator pools running vLLM before verified datasets are fed into MaxText pre-training.

From round-robin to load- and cache-aware routing

With GKE Inference Gateway and llm-d, routing decisions use live serving signals from our vLLM instances rather than static round-robin rotation. GKE Inference Gateway continuously monitors real-time queue depth and key-value (KV) cache utilization across our vLLM endpoints. When a serving node is busy decoding a long equation derivation, the gateway routes incoming requests to nodes with open capacity, so heavy prompts no longer pile up behind busy workers while neighboring nodes sit idle.

At the same time, the gateway routes requests with matching scientific instructions to the serving node where that prefix’s KV cache is already warm in accelerator memory. Because 70% to 80% of each prompt is shared instructional context while the generated reasoning trajectories vary from request to request, combining prefix-cache locality with live queue balancing lets our pods skip repeated prefill work without overloading any single replica.

Higher throughput, predictable training runs

Adopting GKE Inference Gateway powered by llm-d transformed the speed and predictability of our data generation pipeline. Across our production clusters, intelligent routing delivered:

  • 4x higher fleet throughput: Aggregate throughput jumped from 16,964 to 69,114 tokens per second per 1,000 accelerators — growing daily output from 1.47 billion to nearly 6 billion generated tokens.
  • 3.5x to 5.5x gains across individual model pools: Real-time queue balancing kept serving nodes evenly loaded throughout each run, preventing the mid-run slowdowns caused by long reasoning derivations.
  • 14-percentage-point higher prefix-cache hit rate: Routing prompts with matching scientific instructions to warm caches avoided redundant prefill work before each request branched into its own derivation.

For our research and infrastructure teams, the most important outcome was schedule predictability. Quadrupling daily output meant verified datasets were ready on time, so our multi-host pre-training runs started on schedule instead of waiting on data generation.

What’s next for physical AI at ZenteiQ

As we scale our scientific foundation models from 9B to 35B parameters and beyond, we plan to use the same GKE Inference Gateway and llm-d routing setup for post-training reinforcement learning (RL) and automated numerical solver evaluation loops. Because each turn in those multi-turn rollouts builds on the context of the turns before it, they depend even more heavily on live queue balancing and warm prefix caches.

To try these capabilities on your own workloads, explore the GKE Inference Gateway documentation and check out the open-source llm-d project. You can also read how the Gemini platform team cut latency by 35% with GKE Inference Gateway.

entries.content:
Gaurav Soni

Engineering Manager

Jamy Su

Product Manager

For data science, data engineering, and machine learning teams, unlocking the value of unstructured data, such as images, videos, audio, and documents, has historically meant managing siloed data pipelines for structured and unstructured data, and for analytics and AI/ML use cases. Even when files remain in Cloud Storage, running inference requires teams to orchestrate external machine learning workloads, only to face the complex, brittle challenge of stitching those structured inference outputs back into the data warehouse for analysis. This post-hoc data-stitching introduces significant operational overhead and database misalignment.

ObjectRef and multimodal data analytics in BigQuery are now in General Availability (GA), establishing BigQuery as a comprehensive, multimodal agentic data platform.

With ObjectRef, BigQuery natively bridges the gap between Cloud Storage and your analytical engine. You can represent unstructured data as native ObjectRef columns directly alongside your traditional relational columns. This unlocks a massive advantage over standalone model APIs by enabling you to pass multimodal, multi-column inputs directly to Gemini models in a single SQL query or natural language query using conversational analytics. ObjectRef integrations with BigQuery AI, conversational analytics in BigQuery and Gemini Enterprise enable you to easily combine Cloud Storage files with rich, structured database context, metadata, timestamps and custom agent instructions.

You can now leverage BigQuery's core strengths (fully serverless compute, low total cost of ownership, and built-in at-scale inference) to build, run, and govern powerful unstructured-to-structured, unstructured-to-unstructured and fully multimodal-to-multimodal pipelines without separate compute clusters. Crucially, the extracted features and annotations can be combined directly with the unstructured object itself by storing the ObjectRef in the same row. Using this combined data directly in conversational analytics and AI agents avoids the loss of nuanced data and context that typically occurs when customers transform unstructured files into purely structured formats. Customers are already using this approach to generate embeddings for multimodal vector search, perform at-scale classification using GenAI, and execute precise data and feature extraction from vast archives of documents and media, all via standard SQL.

For example, this single query uses AI.AGG to summarize the product images in a public BigQuery sample dataset:

ObjectRef brings structure to the unstructured

ObjectRef is a built-in, predefined STRUCT data type that points to objects outside of BigQuery.

By storing these pointers natively in standard BigQuery tables alongside traditional columns, BigQuery treats unstructured files as first-class data citizens. Furthermore, this architecture supports independent data lifecycles: your GCS data and BigQuery tables can change independently without affecting the underlying data in the other system.

This approach serves multiple data personas by offering powerful advantages:

  • Zero-copy architecture: Keep your high-volume media files securely in Cloud Storage and query them instantly in BigQuery, respecting data gravity and avoiding costly data duplication.
  • SQL and Python interoperability: You can query unstructured data using standard SQL or BigQuery DataFrames. Crucially, you can pass ObjectRefs into BigQuery Python UDFs, allowing you to bring open-source Python libraries, like OpenCV, directly to your data to execute custom logic without moving it.
  • Independent lifecycles and versioning: ObjectRefs ensure reproducible inference by tracking specific GCS generation numbers. If the underlying GCS file changes, your query can still reference the exact version of the file that existed when the row was written.
  • Unified governance: You can secure, audit, and share access to both structured columns and their related unstructured files using BigQuery's existing security policies and IAM controls.

Create full-fidelity ETL with SQL

Since launching ObjectRef in preview, a powerful, highly effective pattern has emerged among our users: building full-fidelity ETL pipelines entirely with SQL.

The diagram below shows the 4 ways to get ObjectRefs for processing unstructured data with BigQuery AI and further querying the multimodal data with AI agents.

Teams are leveraging BigQuery’s serverless architecture to integrate AI/ML directly into their data environments, eliminating the need for separate compute clusters to handle data movement and inference. Managing unstructured data in GCS as standard BigQuery columns allows users to apply core data engineering best practices, such as building idempotent pipelines, ensuring reproducibility, and executing seamless backfills, directly to images, video, audio, and documents.

Once data is robustly prepared, teams use Gemini within BigQuery to execute full-fidelity ETL. They unlock dual-layer analytics by extracting features and annotating unstructured data while keeping the original ObjectRef anchored in the same row. The structured outputs power fast filtering, reporting and BI dashboards, while the attached unstructured objects remain available for deep, context-heavy reasoning. For example, you might extract sentiment scores and topic tags from an archive of customer call recordings to quickly flag at-risk accounts on a BI dashboard (the structured layer). Simultaneously, a conversational analytics agent evaluating escalation processes can seamlessly fall back to the original audio files to analyze the caller and customer service representative interactions, preventing the loss of critical nuance that typically occurs in unstructured-to-structured ETL pipelines.

Proven use cases from industry leaders

“At Snap, the safety of our community is a top priority, and we aim to limit users’ exposure to content that violates our Community Guidelines. We regularly review samples of public posts, and by leveraging ObjectRef with BigQuery AI, we transitioned from simple random sampling to post-stratification sampling. This transition improved the efficiency of our human review processes, enabling us to reinvest reclaimed capacity into new and expanded workflows that further enhance our ability to detect and address potentially harmful content.” - Carlos Ortiz, Data Scientist, Snap

During the preview phase, we saw adoption across a variety of critical workloads. Customers have successfully transitioned these experimental pipelines into production, transforming unstructured data into actionable, structured insights:

  • Content moderation: Online platforms leverage BigQuery to integrate multimedia assets with standard telemetry data in a single pipeline to fundamentally enhance their moderation and safety outcomes.

  • Proactive threat detection: Enterprise security teams use BigQuery to analyze visual and structural web components alongside network logs, driving critical advancements in proactive threat identification.

  • Inventory compliance: Online retailers extract text and context directly from vast image repositories to automatically flag regulatory or brand compliance issues at scale.

  • Customer experience: Service-oriented enterprises analyze audio interactions between support agents and customers with BigQuery AI to evaluate customer sentiment and improve service delivery.

New in GA

We streamlined the developer experience for the General Availability release, focusing on support for a wide variety of customer use cases:

  • Flexible authentication:

    • In GA, we introduced End User Credentials (EUC) support for ObjectRefs. Users can now quickly query and explore unstructured data using their personal IAM identity directly for ad-hoc analysis.

    • In preview, querying unstructured files required setting up explicit BigQuery connections for ObjectRefs. While these connections remain fully supported and are the recommended best practice for robust, service-account-driven production pipelines, we recognize they require additional setup.

  • Unified support for your Cloud Storage metadata: We know your unstructured data’s metadata lives in various places across Google Cloud, and ObjectRef now supports all of them.

    • If it's already in a table: Whether your metadata currently resides in BigQuery object tables, Cloud Storage insights datasets, or simply as raw string URIs within standard BigQuery tables, you can seamlessly create and manage ObjectRefs to analyze the underlying data.

    • If it isn't in a table: The new 
      OBJ.LIST
      function lists files directly from a Cloud Storage path and returns an 
      ObjectRef
      for each one, so you don't need to create a table first.

  • Array support for comparative analytics: We introduced native support for processing ObjectRefs contained within arrays. This enables entirely new classes of workloads, such as comparing multiple documents against one another, analyzing sequences of images, or batching items in a single semantic call.

See it in action: End-to-end multimodal analytics

To illustrate the power of these GA updates, let's look at how you can build real-world, multimodal pipelines using our streamlined SQL operators.

1. Full-fidelity ETL: Call center audio analysis

Analyzing customer service calls historically required moving audio files to specialized transcription and natural language processing clusters. With ObjectRef, you can parse audio files, extract structured business intelligence and add them directly as standard relational columns.

Use the GA OBJ.MAKE_REF() function to automatically detect the audio format from a raw string URI and BigQuery’s managed AI functions for well known use-cases. For example, you can use AI.CLASSIFY() to categorize customer call types. By default, BigQuery uses Optimized Mode for AI Functions to reduce the number of tokens consumed.

This table can serve as a multimodal data source for a BigQuery conversational analytics agent. The agent translates natural language queries into SQL using BigQuery AI functions to analyze audio files when additional information is needed.

Go to the Agents tab in BigQuery to create a conversational analytics agent and select your multimodal table as a source.

2. At-scale gen AI filtering: Product compliance

Optimized Modereduces the number of tokens consumed to further optimize your workloads.

3. Ad-hoc discovery: Product catalog enrichment

4. Multi-object reasoning: Proactive threat detection

Start analyzing today

BigQuery ObjectRef is now generally available on all BigQuery editions and on-demand pricing tiers.

If you are currently managing complex, fragmented infrastructure just to perform machine learning inference on your Cloud Storage files, it's time to consolidate. Bring AI directly to your storage. Start leveraging your existing data engineering practices to build robust, scalable, and secure multimodal analytics pipelines directly within BigQuery.

To get started with ObjectRef and multimodal analytics, check out these resources:

  • Walk through our hands-on tutorial to generate image captions and assign product categories using synthetic data.
  • Watch live demos from Cloud Next about unifying unstructured and structured data, and generating text with LLMs and performing vector search.
  • Learn how to work with ObjectRef in the BigQuery documentation.

entries.content:
Chris Betz

CISO, Google Cloud

Raluca Ada Popa

Head of Gemini Security, Google DeepMind

Editor's note: This blog was updated on Oct. 23, 2026 at 3:20 p.m. PDT, with additional guidance from Mandiant Consulting on monitoring, patching, and remediation. We have previously updated the blog on Oct. 22, 2026, with revised guidance for Security Command Center and Cloud Armor, and on Oct. 21, 2026.

PHP and Wiz Research disclosed today two critical vulnerabilities in the core PHP language runtime that can expose applications to unauthenticated remote code execution and memory disclosure. Wiz used a mix of models to identify and help remediate these vulnerabilities.

Notably, Gemini 4 Argon made an invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability, exploit development, attack detection, and validation of the patch.

While Google Cloud itself is not vulnerable, users of PHP running on Google Cloud may be vulnerable. At Google Cloud, we understand the severity of these vulnerabilities, and are sharing guidance to help our customers take immediate action to secure their applications.

Vulnerability background

PHP is a widely-used, server-side scripting language that powers many websites, content management systems, and web applications. On Oct. 21, 2026, CVE.org assigned the vulnerabilities as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

The official Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) base severity score for each of the PHP flaws has been determined as Critical, a severity of 9.2. Generally, this ranking means that threat actors can crash and hijack the affected system, and can easily steal, alter, and wipe its data — although mitigating circumstances can make it harder to exploit the flaw.

  • CVE-2026-109618: Out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid.

  • CVE-2026-109619: Request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.

  • Vulnerable versions: All versions of PHP from 5.4 through 8.5.11

  • Patched in: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35

  • Not patched: The PHP project is not releasing fixes for PHP 8.1 or earlier, which have reached end of life.

  • Fix: CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w) and CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp):

  • Announcement: PHP has published a security advisory on these two vulnerabilities.

Wiz Research has published a detailed description of the research and the coordinated disclosure process.

Update PHP and redeploy your applications

We urge all customers running PHP applications on Google Cloud to immediately update to PHP 8.2 or newer, and redeploy their services using a patched version.

This applies specifically to applications deployed on:

  • App Engine standard environment: Supported runtimes are patched automatically. If you are on PHP 8.1 or earlier, upgrade to PHP 8.2 or newer and redeploy.

  • App Engine flexible environment: Redeploy your PHP runtimes using a supported runtime. If you are using a custom runtime, update your PHP dependencies to a patched version and redeploy your application.

  • Cloud Run: If automatic base image updates are not enabled, or you deploy your own container image, rebuild with a patched version of PHP and redeploy.

  • Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE): Update your container images with a patched version of PHP and redeploy your pods.

  • Google Cloud Marketplace: If you run a Marketplace solution that includes PHP, such as a content management system or LAMP stack, apply the update from the solution provider or update PHP directly.

Automatic patches for serverless platforms

Google Cloud is rolling out updated serverless base images for all supported PHP versions on App Engine Standard, App Engine Flexible, Cloud Run, Cloud Run function, and Cloud Functions for Firebase.

What this means for you:

  • App Engine standard environment (PHP 8.2 and newer): Applications are updated automatically. No action is required.

  • App Engine flexible environment (all PHP versions): Applications are not updated automatically. Redeploy your application as soon as possible to PHP 8.2 and newer.

  • Cloud Run functions (PHP 8.2 and newer): Functions with automatic base image updates enabled are updated automatically. Functions without automatic base image updates enabled must be redeployed.

  • Cloud Run (PHP 8.2 and newer): Services with automatic base image updates enabled are updated automatically. Services built without automatic base image updates must be rebuilt and redeployed to pick up the patched runtime.

Important considerations:

  • Unsupported runtimes will not be patched. The upstream PHP project is not backporting these fixes to PHP 8.1 or earlier. Applications on PHP 5.5, PHP 7.2, PHP 7.3, PHP 7.4, or PHP 8.1 remain vulnerable and must be upgraded to PHP 8.2 or newer. See the following runtime support schedules for serverless lifecycle dates:

  • Container images you build yourself are your responsibility. If you have deployed your own container image to Cloud Run or App Engine Flexible (such as with a custom runtime), rebuild it with a patched version of PHP and redeploy.

  • Capture memory forensics before restarting suspect hosts: If a server shows signs of active probing or anomalous 

    PHPSESSID
    cookies, capture worker memory before patching or rebooting, as restarting workers permanently destroys volatile heap evidence.

  • Restart the actual web-serving SAPI (including supervisor-managed workers): Upgrading packages on disk leaves vulnerable 

    libphp.so
    or 
    php-fpm
    binaries resident in running worker processes. Explicitly restart 
    php8.x-fpm
    , 
    apache2
    /
    httpd
    , 
    frankenphp
    , or 
    lsws
    . 

  • Do not wait on volunteer third-party RPM mirrors: The PHP security team noted that third-party mirrors may lag behind coordinated disclosure; use official distro security repositories (verify via 

    apt-get changelog php-fpm
    or 
    rpm -q --changelog php-fpm | grep -E "CVE-2026-109618|CVE-2026-109619"
    ) or official source builds.

  • Audit and mitigate enterprise edge and management infrastructure: Inventory all edge, gateway, management, storage, and security systems, which frequently embed PHP in administrative control planes or core OS modules. As vendors continue disclosing vulnerabilities, coordinate immediately with manufacturers to apply emergency firmware updates or approved temporary workarounds.

Mitigating CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 with Cloud Armor

Cloud Armor has issued recommended mitigations that use Cloud Armor managed rules. Customers with active managed rules do not need to take action; protection against these vulnerabilities is applied automatically.

If you have not yet deployed Cloud Armor managed rules, doing so now can still help you mitigate these vulnerabilities. The Cloud Armor managed rules protections are available now through automatically-updated threat intelligence rulesets.

These rules are intended to help protect your internet-facing PHP applications and services that use global or regional application load balancers. Follow these steps to deploy the rules immediately as a frontline defense-in-depth mitigation while your vulnerability management program updates and verifies all vulnerable PHP instances in your environment.

1. Deploying stable managed rules in enforce mode for automatic updates:

To protect your workloads, follow this guide to enable the File Upload and RFI categories. We recommend that you configure all ruleset categories in the stable version in enforced mode.

2. Mitigate risk on request bodies that exceed configured inspection limits:

Create a rule in your security policies to help ensure that no uninspected or unnecessarily large content reaches your backends. This is important for these CVEs, because threat actors may use large payloads to trigger out-of-memory conditions. 

Verifying WAF rule safety for your application and consuming telemetry

Consult our Cloud Armor best practices guide and account for service limitations to minimize risk and optimize performance.

Cloud Armor mitigations serve solely as compensating controls in your layered defense to reduce immediate exposure. Upgrading PHP to a fixed version and redeploying services is required to fully resolve these vulnerabilities.

Monitoring and auditing

Google Cloud and Wiz are currently supporting customers with active monitoring, auditing, and runtime detection across its native security offerings. Customers can use:

  • On-Demand Scanning API to manually scan images stored locally on your computer or remotely in Artifact Registry. Customers using Artifact Analysis will be notified of these vulnerabilities on both new and existing artifacts to identify at-risk workloads.

  • Security Command Center to monitor workloads and identify externally exposed instances affected by these two CVEs.

  • External exposure: Enable the External Exposure service with the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_RCE_VULNERABILITY scanning module to detect exposed PHP workloads across Compute Engine, GKE, and Cloud Run.  Findings show the Google Cloud native path across load balancers, Cloud Armor policies, and firewall rules to help you verify WAF coverage and block untrusted firewall access while patching.

  • Vulnerability assessment: Enable Vulnerability Assessment for your organization or projects to find out if your Compute Engine VMs, GKE nodes, and container workloads are running PHP versions vulnerable to PHP2Shell.

  • Threat Detection: Enable Container Threat Detection for GKE and Cloud Run Threat detection to monitor your workloads for intrusions.

  • Google Security Operations now has 23 new curated detections added to the Mandiant Frontline Threats rule pack. We recommend verifying that this rule pack is enabled and reviewing your detections to assess any potential impact to your environment. 

  • Enterprise Plus customers can additionally use the Emerging Threat Center and search for “GLOBAL.26.015” for further details. Enterprise plus customers who have enabled the Threat Hunt Agent in Public Preview can also perform a hunt on GLOBAL.26.015 from the Emerging Threats Center.

  • Wiz customers can refer to the Wiz Threat Intel Center advisory for PHP2Shell, which includes built-in coverage for agentless and runtime vulnerability detection, exploitation detection via Wiz Defend and Sensor, and automatic response policies, alongside remediation and threat hunting guidance. More information is available here on response steps with Wiz.

Additionally, Mandiant Threat Defense is actively supporting customers by monitoring curated detections in Google Security Operations and hunting for evidence of intrusion activity related to this campaign.

Patching and remediation

The PHP security release has been published. You should update PHP across every server environment, container image, and deployment pipeline. In addition:

  • As part of Wiz's zero-day response commitment, WizOS PHP images are available at zero billable units for all customers for the next 60 days. WizOS PHP base images, both standard Alpine-hardened and FIPS-compliant builds, are already patched against CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, built from source.

  • Wiz customers can use the Green Agent to translate the PHP2Shell Threat Intel advisory into resource-tailored remediation guidance, including prescribing the correct PHP patch versions, identifying the right WAF mitigations, recommending opportunities to swap in for hardened WizOS PHP images, and suggesting enabling runtime blocking where there are gaps.

Prepatch PHP runtime hardening

If you can not upgrade every binary immediately, apply the following settings in your master startup php.ini or static FPM pool configuration (

php_admin_value
/ 
php_admin_flag
) and restart all workers.
  •  Put all settings in the main php.ini file: Avoid defining per-request settings in 
    .htaccess
    or web server configurations. Warnings triggered while loading these temporary settings run too early and can activate vulnerable code paths. Moving all options into the global 
    php.ini
    can prevent this.

  • Restart workers after each request (pm.max_requests = 1): Certain attacks require reusing a worker process across multiple requests. Setting 

    pm.max_requests = 1
    in 
    www.conf
    forces worker processes to reset after every request, blocking multi-step memory attacks.

  • Hiding error messages is not enough: Simply setting 

    display_errors = Off
    does not fully block memory leak attacks. Modern exploits can extract sensitive memory directly through extra-large session cookies or specific error pages, even when standard error display is disabled.

Edge proxy and WAF controls

Because RFC 1867 multipart parsing occurs before script execution, reverse proxies and WAFs serve as critical frontline defenses. To defend against recent PoCs, edge controls should focus on mitigating four key evasion techniques:

  • Block multipart/form-data on non-upload routes: Block multipart requests where file uploads are not needed. Ensure WAF regexes match commas and whitespace before 

    boundary=
    (e.g., 
    (?i)^\s*multipart/form-data(?:[\s,;]|$)
    ) to prevent delimiter evasion in PHP's RFC 1867 parser.

  • Reject chunked transfer encoding and restrict body complexity: Reject 

    Transfer-Encoding: chunked
    POST requests, enforce 
    client_max_body_size 8m;
    , block deeply nested bracket field names (
    name\s*=\s*"?[^"\r\n]*(\[[^\]]*\]){8,}
    ), and cap headers per multipart part (
    <= 128
    ) to prevent heap amplification.

  • Enforce strict cookie format and body size limits: Block 

    PHPSESSID
    cookies containing null bytes or non-alphanumeric characters outside 
    ^[A-Za-z0-9,-]{22,256}$
    . Enforce strict request body size caps on non-upload routes to stop large multipart padding that bypasses WAF inspection windows.

  • Enforce ingress restrictions: Limit ingress to vulnerable or unpatched public resources only from WAF. Consider additional network ingress restrictions or taking vulnerable web servers offline until patched.

Operating system sandboxing and detections

Because native use-after-free execution runs inside the worker process — allowing RCE payloads to bypass PHP security settings — robust operating system containment and network monitoring remain critical across both pre-patch and post-patch phases.

  • Read-only web roots and systemd/container Cgroup limits: Execute PHP workers using a dedicated unprivileged account with read-only access across all document roots (via 

    ProtectSystem=strict
    in systemd or 
    readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
    in Kubernetes) alongside 
    NoNewPrivileges=yes
    .

    Limit total worker memory using cgroups (e.g., 

    MemoryMax=2G
    ) instead of 
    LimitAS=
    or 
    ulimit -v
    , which cause 
    mmap()
    to return 
    NULL
    and trigger the vulnerable out-of-memory path.

  • Block network connections and restrict process execution: Block outbound internet access from PHP servers using network security rules to stop attackers from downloading malicious files or creating remote shells. Additionally, use process security controls or runtime monitoring to prevent PHP from executing command-line shell tools like 

    /bin/sh
    , 
    curl
    , or 
    wget
    .
